newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Diverse diet of deals.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Diverse diet of deals.

text.p: Asian debt markets offered a diverse diet on Thursday.
Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi launched through its Hong Kong branch a HK$2.0 billion floating rate certificate of deposit issue via lead arranger Tokyo-Mitsubishi International.
The three-year FRCDs pay a coupon of 20 basis points and, with fees, an all-in return of 25 basis points to top-tier participants.
The response to the deal was generally favorable.
"It's very attractive and we will probably join it. Pricing might be a bit low but it's a good quality issue," said one syndicate manager.
Application will be made to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to accept the certificates as eligible for its Liquidity Adjustment Facility, or discount window.
Eligibility for LAF makes an issue more attractive to banks because holders of the qualifying debt can engage in repurchase agreements with the monetary authority, increasing liquidity.
The issue is expected to be rated A1 by Moody's Investors Service.

Bankers said the issue is comparable to a LAF-eligible deal launched by A1-rated Fuji Bank in April. Those certificates, which are due in April 1999, paid an all-in of 28 basis points and are now trading at 22 basis points.
In other news from Hong Kong, the HK$1.5 billion global bond launched on Wednesday for U.S. mortgage agency Fannie Mae is now free to trade.
The deal, which was jointly lead managed by HSBC Markets and Merrill Lynch International, was the first-ever Hong Kong dollar global bond.

In news of Indonesia, Merrill Lynch announced terms on a 144a bond with registration rights for Pratama Datakom Asia BV. The US$260 million bond is guaranteed by Indonesian multimedia firm PT Datakom.
The callable bond has a final maturity of eight years. It pays a semi-annual coupon of 12.75 percent, offering a yield pick-up of more than 600 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Malaysian company Perwaja Terengganu's recently launched US$400 million floating rate note issue has been withdrawn, but another deal is planned.
The issue, which was guaranteed by the government of Malaysia, was withdrawn by the issuer and the guarantor, arranger Standard Chartered Bank said on Thursday.
Standard Chartered Bank has been mandated to arrange a new FRN issue with amended terms and conditions, the bank said.
The issue that was withdrawn had a final maturity of five years. It paid a coupon of 22 basis points and five basis points in fees.
A new issue could be launched as early as Friday.

Perwaja is a loss-making state-owned steel maker that the Malaysian government is now trying to privatize. Despite the company's difficulties, bankers have shown some interest in the transaction because of the government guarantee. Investment-grade Malaysia generally is very popular with investors.
Bankers speculated that the issuer and the guarantor may have pulled the deal with the idea of negotiating more advantageous terms.
